title: Tracking Performance in Endurance Racing Sports: Evaluation of the Accuracy Offered by Three Commercial GNSS Receivers Aimed at the Sports Market
authors: Gloersen O, Kocbach J, Gilgien M
population: Six volunteers skiing four laps of a 3.05 km cross-country track wearing a 1 Hz wrist GNSS (Garmin Forerunner 920XT), a 10 Hz standalone receiver (Catapult Optimeye S5) and a 10 Hz differential receiver (ZXY-Go), against a geodetic reference (< 5 cm)
findings: Horizontal position error (Q3) was 5.29 m for the Garmin 920XT vs 1.04 m (Catapult S5) and 2.09 m (ZXY-Go); vertical precision (IQR) was 13.35 m for the Garmin vs 3.89 and 2.71 m.
Horizontal speed precision (IQR) was 0.66 m/s for the Garmin vs 0.072 and 0.038 m/s for the 10 Hz receivers.
Error was inversely related to speed, so substantially larger errors can occur at the low speeds typical of uphill skiing.
All receivers produced sub-second accuracy in the time analysis except at very low speeds.
limitations: Cross-country skiing, not running; six volunteers; one older (2014-era) wrist watch; measures position, speed and time, not total distance accuracy. Applicable to running only by analogy.
implications: Do not derive instantaneous or gradient-adjusted pace from raw 1 Hz wrist GNSS speed; smooth speed and prefer device-reported lap/total distance, and treat watch elevation as noisy.
Weight pace-based intensity less on slow uphill or technical segments, where speed error is largest; use HR or RPE there. Applicability is indirect, so treat as grade D.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, Front Physiol, 9 Oct 2018, first author Gloersen. Numbers match the abstract (vertical IQRs for ZXY-Go/CAT-S5/Gar are 2.71/3.89/13.35 m). Evidence level lowered from C to D because the sport, sample and device are all indirect to modern running. No running-specific GPS systematic review was found.
